analysis.one_liner: Shuts down an immigration detention center in Newark and bars any new contract to run it.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 6, 2026, the bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee and has taken no further action; Congress remains in session.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Department of Homeland Security to stop all immigration detention operations at Delaney Hall, a detention center in Newark, New Jersey, within 90 days of becoming law. It also forbids the department from signing any new contract to run the facility, and requires it to terminate the existing operating contract. If the government terminates the contract, it only has to pay for services already performed.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants detained at Delaney Hall and their families, who would no longer be held at the facility and could not be placed there in the future. People held there are often awaiting immigration hearings near New York and New Jersey, so closure would spare them and their relatives and lawyers from detention at that site.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrant detainees and their New Jersey families

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to cease all immigration detention operations at Delaney Hall no later than 90 days after enactment [S2]
Bars the department from entering any new contract or agreement to operate the facility for detention [S2]
Requires termination of the existing operating contract for the government's convenience, limiting taxpayer liability to payment for services rendered before termination takes effect [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The private company that operates Delaney Hall under a federal detention contract loses the facility and any future business there. The administration also loses one detention site, which enforcement supporters say would force detainees to be held elsewhere or reduce holding capacity in the region.
analysis.who_pays_short: The facility's private operator and ICE

drawbacks.text: Closing a detention site reduces holding capacity in the New York area; enforcement supporters argue people facing deportation proceedings would have to be detained farther away, at sites harder for families and lawyers to reach [S2]
The bill targets a single facility rather than the nationwide detention system, so detainees moved out of Delaney Hall could face the same conditions elsewhere, limiting the practical benefit [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people detained at Delaney Hall and their families, ending operations there is a real benefit, and the bill is written to keep the closure cheap by limiting contract-termination liability. The cost is regional: one detention site disappears, and enforcement capacity advocates lose a facility they consider needed. The narrower weakness is that a single-facility bill does not change conditions across the detention network.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it sits with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined by Sen. Andy Kim [S2]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S4]
The bill has one cosponsor in addition to the sponsor [S3]
No further action has been taken, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027 [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: the facility's private operator keeps running Delaney Hall and the detention system continues as before, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The detention operator keeps its contract, so far

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to close Delaney Hall

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters are New Jersey Democrats; no one has acted against the bill in the record and no vote has been held.

industries.note: Private operators run ICE detention centers under federal contracts and earn revenue per detainee-day held, so barring new contracts and terminating the existing one ends that revenue stream at Delaney Hall. The bill's termination-for-convenience provision limits what the operator can collect afterward.

industries.industry: Immigration enforcement contractors and detention services
industries.note: The bill removes one facility from the detention network, shrinking the pool of sites available to hold immigrants in federal custody in the New York region.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor, no committee action, and sits in a committee controlled by the majority party, with the Congress ending January 3, 2027. Single-facility bills from the minority party at this stage almost never get a hearing or a floor vote, so the likely outcome is that it expires at the end of this Congress.
